'''''Commelina erecta''''', commonly known as '''white mouth dayflower''', '''slender dayflower,''' or '''widow's tears.'''<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Blousel Blommetjie data - Encyclopedia of Life |url=https://eol.org/pages/1122761/data |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230218215053/https://eol.org/pages/1122761/data |archive-date=2023-02-18 |access-date=2025-11-18 |website=eol.org |language=en}}</ref> C. erecta is a blue flower often recognized by its two large blue petals and smaller white petal. It is a perennial herb common across the world and native throughout the [[Americas]], [[Africa]] and western [[Asia]].<ref name=":3" />

== Description ==
=== Flowers ===
''C. erecta'' is a [[perennial]] flower recognized by its two large blue petals and smaller third petal.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=coer |access-date=2025-11-09 |website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref> Due to its three petal arrangement it is botanically recognized as a [[Monocotyledon|monocot]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Monocot_vs_Dicot {{!}} Organismal Biology |url=https://organismalbio.biosci.gatech.edu/growth-and-reproduction/plant-development-i-tissue-differentiation-and-function/monocot_vs_dicot/ |access-date=2025-11-18 |website=organismalbio.biosci.gatech.edu}}</ref> The two larger blue petals are located at the top of the plant with the third white petal in between and below them. The full flower is three-quarters to one and a quarter inches across.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Commelina erecta (Slender Dayflower): Minnesota Wildflowers |url=https://www.minnesotawildflowers.info/flower/slender-dayflower |access-date=2025-11-18 |website=www.minnesotawildflowers.info |language=en}}</ref> Each flower only lasts for a Day earning it the nickname the [[Dayflower]]. However, the buds on the plant may bloom 3–4 days apart increasing the individual's time in blossom.<ref name=":02" />

Between the petals are the [[Staminode|staminoide]], central stamen, lateral stamen, and style. ''Commelina e.'' exhibits [[Glossary of botanical terms|enantiostyly]] meaning the flowers have two [[Polymorphism (biology)|morphs]] that are mirror images of each other where the style points either left or right.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Contreras-Varela |first1=Ximena |last2=García-Franco |first2=José G. |last3=Aguirre-Jaimes |first3=Armando |date=2023-05-01 |title=Floral and reproductive biology of Commelina erecta L. (Commelinaceae) in a coastal dune system on the Gulf of Mexico |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S036725302300049X |journal=Flora |volume=302 |bibcode=2023FMDFE.30252259C |doi=10.1016/j.flora.2023.152259 |issn=0367-2530 |article-number=152259}}</ref> However [[Glossary of botanical terms|enantiostyly]] makes up only two of the three [[Polymorphism (biology)|polymorphs]] of this flower. The third [[Polymorphism (biology)|polymorph]] is a male flower that completely lacks the style.<ref name=":2" />

=== Leaves ===
The leaves are lance-linear (long and thin) with a pointed apex and round base. The margins or edges of the leaf may be red. The leaves form sheaths around the stem with small hairs at their bases. All of the leaves have parallel longitudinal [[Venation (botany)|venation]].<ref name=":2" />

Below the flower are both its [[sepal]]s and [[spathe]]. The [[Bract|spathe]] structure is made up of a leaf that grows folded in half lengthwise below the site of floral growth. This leaf is sealed from its [[Leaf|apex]] to stem leaving only an opening at the top for the flower to emerge. The bract is covered in small short hairs.<ref name=":1" />

=== Stems ===
''C. erecta'' grows laterally across the ground reaching up to three feet long, yet it may grow vertically if structurally supported by another plant.<ref name=":02" /> The stems are generally rough, but can occasionally be smooth and form many branches.<ref name=":1" />

=== Fruit ===
''Commelina e''. forms a three [[carpellate]] fruit; meaning it has three ovules and may form a seed from each ovule.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Panigo |first1=Elisa Soledad |last2=Oggero |first2=Eugenia |last3=Dellaferrera |first3=Ignacio Miguel |last4=Alesso |first4=Carlos Agustín |last5=Chantre |first5=Guillermo Rubén |last6=Perreta |first6=Mariel Gladis |last7=Reutemann |first7=Andrea Guadalupe |date=March 2024 |title=Fruit dehiscence mechanism and release of dimorphic seeds with different germination properties in Commelina erecta |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00709-023-01904-z |journal=Protoplasma |language=en |volume=261 |issue=2 |pages=377–393 |bibcode=2024Prpls.261..377P |doi=10.1007/s00709-023-01904-z |issn=0033-183X |pmid=37910229}}</ref> The fruit typically appears green and can have a smooth to slightly granular surface.<ref name=":6" />

== Taxonomy ==
''Commelina erecta'' was named by Charles Plumier to honor the two Botanists of Commelin family [[Caspar Commelijn|Caspar]] and [[Jan Commelin|Jan]] as well as a third family member who died before accomplishing anything in botany.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Knapp |first=Sandra |title=In the Name of Plants: From Attenborough to Washington, the People behind Plant Names |date=November 2, 2022 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=9780226824314 |location=Chicago |pages=35}}</ref> Plumier intended the two prominent petals of the flower to represent [[Caspar Commelijn|Caspar Commelin]] and [[Jan Commelin]] and for the third diminished petal to represent to unnamed dead Commelin.<ref name=":7" /> ''C. erecta'' was officially established as a species in 1753 when [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] published it in the [[Species Plantarum|Species Planetarium]].<ref name=":7" />

''C. erecta h''as seven 'children' including different [[Variety (botany)|varieties]], [[Form (botany)|formae]], and [[subspecies]]. The subspecies are Commelina erecta subsp. erecta, Commelina erecta subsp. livingstonii, and Commelina erecta subsp. maritima. The variants are Commelina erecta var. angustifolia (Michx.) and Commelina erecta var. deamiana. Finally, the forma Commelina erecta f. dielsii (Herter) Bacig and Commelina erecta f. roseopurpurea (Herter) Bacig.<ref name=":3" />

Due to its wide geographical range it has many common names across different languages. In Uruguay it is known as Yerba de Santa Lucı́.<ref name=":32">{{Cite journal |last1=Cerdeiras |first1=M. P. |last2=Pianzzola |first2=M. J. |last3=Vázquez |first3=A. |date=2001-05-01 |title=The antibacterial activity of Commelina erecta extracts |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0924857901003132 |journal=International Journal of Antimicrobial Agents |volume=17 |issue=5 |pages=423–424 |doi=10.1016/S0924-8579(01)00313-2 |issn=0924-8579 |pmid=11337233}}</ref> In [[Afrikaans|Africaans]], ''C. erecta's'' preferred name is Blousel Blommetjie.<ref name=":3" />

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Commelina erecta'' is native to much of the world, including the Americas, [[Africa]] and [[West Asia|western Asia]]. In the Americas it is present in the [[United States]], the [[West Indies]], every country of [[Central America]] and south through the tropics into [[Argentina]]. In the [[United States]] it can be found from [[South Dakota]] and [[Pennsylvania]] down to [[Florida]] and [[Texas]].<ref name=":4">Lloyd-Reilley, J. & Maher, S. D. & Kadin, E. (2002). ''ERECT DAYFLOWER Commelina erecta var. angustifolia (Michx.) Fern.'' [PDF]. United States Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Conservation Service. https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/factsheet/pdf/fs_coera.pdf</ref>

In the West Indies it is present throughout [[Puerto Rico]] and on several of the [[Virgin Islands]] such as [[Saint Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands|Saint Croix]], [[Saint Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands|Saint Thomas]], [[Saint John, U.S. Virgin Islands|Saint John]], [[George Dog Island]], [[Anegada]], [[Great Camanoe]], [[Guana Island]], [[Tortola]] and [[Water Island, U.S. Virgin Islands|Water Island]].<ref name=":3" />

The plant is also widespread though. In west Africa it is present in [[Senegal]], [[Guinea]], [[Guinea-Bissau]], [[Sierra Leone]], [[Liberia]], the [[Ivory Coast]], [[Ghana]], [[Burkina Faso]], [[Benin]], [[Nigeria]], and [[Bioko]].<ref name=":3" />

It can grow in a wide range of habitats, both natural and disturbed, including prairies, streambanks, gardens, and roadsides.<ref name=":02" />

=== Ecology ===
[[File:Trapoeraba (Commelina Erecta).jpg|thumb|422x422px|Fly preparing to pollinate ''C. erecta'']]
In North America'', C. erecta'' is often eaten by the [[Northern bobwhite|Bobwhite Quail]] (Northern Bobwhite) the [[Lesser prairie-chicken|Lesser Prairie-Chicken]], [[white-tailed deer]], and cattle.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /> ''C. erecta'' is often pollinated and visited by flies and bees including [[Hoverfly|Syrphid flies]], [[Melissodes bimaculatus|Two-spotted Long-horned Bees]], [[Lasioglossum nymphale]], [[Augochlora|Pure Green Augochlora]], and [[Augochloropsis metallica|Green Metallic Sweat Bees]].<ref name=":3" /> ''C.'' erecta can also be parasitized by ''[[Liriomyza commelinae]]''.<ref name=":3" />

== Uses ==
''C. erecta'' is a wild edible plant and is consumed by many groups of people across its distribution. It is also used as a traditional medicine is some groups. ''C. erecta'' is commonly consumed and used as a [[traditional medicine]] in Brazil, and analysis of its [[bioactive compound]]s shows that can act as an [[antioxidant]], [[antibacterial]], [[antifungal]], and [[anti-inflammatory]] agent.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cavichi |first1=Lucas Vinicius |last2=Liberal |first2=Ângela |last3=Dias |first3=Maria Inês |last4=Mandim |first4=Filipa |last5=Pinela |first5=José |last6=Kostić |first6=Marina |last7=Soković |first7=Marina |last8=Kalschne |first8=Daneysa Lahis |last9=Fernandes |first9=Ângela |last10=Canan |first10=Cristiane |last11=Barros |first11=Lillian |last12=Amaral |first12=Joana S. |date=January 2023 |title=Chemical Composition and Biological Activity of Commelina erecta: An Edible Wild Plant Consumed in Brazil |url=https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/12/1/192 |journal=Foods |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |doi=10.3390/food |doi-broken-date=19 November 2025 |issn=2304-8158 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250903113728/https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/12/1/192 |archive-date=2025-09-03 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":32" />

In [[Uruguay]], it is commonly made into a juice to treat eye infections.<ref name=":32" /> ''C. erecta'' is also used by the [[Seminole]] to sooth irritation.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sturtevant |first=William C. |url=https://ehrafworldcultures.yale.edu/cultures/nn16/documents/046 |title=The Mikasuki Seminole: medical beliefs and practices |date=1989 |publisher=University Microfilms International |language=en |orig-date=1955}}</ref>

=== Cultivation ===
''C. erecta'' typically blooms in North America from May to October. It grows best in partial shade in dry sandy soil. ''C. erecta'' can be grown by seed or by transplanting tubers.<ref name=":02" /> ''C. erecta'' is widely considered a weed across its domain and can be invasive so planting should be done carefully.<ref name=":4" />
